plan.english: He put a name on him.

cognate_refs.locus: Eznik, Ełc ałandocʻ II.3 §24 (DMHP, Eznik text)
Vuk, Srpske narodne pjesme, 'Nahod Simeun' l. 16 (serbian-vuk-wikisource, pageid 13012)

notes: 'Put a name (on someone, dative)', *h₁nómn̥ dʰeh₁-: West 2007 ch. 10 lists Hitt. lāman dāi-, Ved. nā́ma dhā-, Av. nāmąn dā-, Gk ὄνομα τίθεσθαι, Lat. indere nomen, Toch. A ñom tā-, B ñem tā-, Serbo-Croat ime djesti (after Schmitt). This line adds Armenian, which West does not cite, and a Slavic locus. fame-013 carries the same formula on other loci (Hittite, RV 5.3.10, Od. 18.5, Plautus), so the two belong in one eval group. Parallels, all checked locally: Armenian, Eznik II.3 §24 (DMHP) yaṙaǰ kʻan zcnaneln dnēr nma anun Ormizd 'before the birth he put on him the name Ormizd' (Zurvan naming his unborn son; imperfect of dnem < *dʰeh₁-, dative nma of the anaphoric na, anun < *h₁nómn̥). Serbo-Croatian, Vuk 'Nahod Simeun' l. 16 lijepo mu ime nađenuo 'he put a fine name on him' (na-djenuti, Slavic *dě- < *dʰeh₁- with the -nǫ- perfective; dative enclitic mu). Greek, Od. 19.403–404 ὄνομ' εὕρεο ὅττι κε θῆαι / παιδὸς παιδὶ φίλῳ 'find a name to put on your child's child' (aor. subj. middle + dative; AGDT). Vedic, AVŚ 3.13.3 tasmād vār nāma vo hitam 'therefore "vār" is the name put on you' (the -tá- participle of dhā- + dative vaḥ; DCS). Late witness: the Vuk song is a 19th-century oral record, valid for the wording only. It is cited as 'Serbo-Croatian'; it is the line's only Balto-Slavic witness, so the branch count is not inflated. The builder has no reflexes for that language, so SC ime (= *h₁nómn̥) is not counted. Secure: *h₁nómn̥, exact in Armenian, Greek and Vedic. The verb is shared at root level only: the engine's root aorist dʰéh₁t is the formation of the Armenian aorist ed- (of dnem) and Ved. ádhāt, but the cited passages have the Armenian imperfect of the nasal present, the Slavic -nǫ- perfective, a Greek middle aorist subjunctive and a Vedic participle. Tense: aorist for the single act, as in fame-013. Voice: active, with Armenian, Serbo-Croatian and Vedic (Greek has the middle). Interpolated: the dative pronoun (Arm. nma and SC mu are anaphoric datives like the engine's; Greek has a noun, Vedic the 2pl). The engine's primary dative h₁ésmey has *-ey; Ved. asmai points to *h₁ésmōy, which the engine lists as the alternative form.

cognate_refs.locus: Slovo o polku Igoreve 77 (TOROT spi, citation part 77)

notes: Polyptoton 'brother to brother' framing speech. West 2007 ch. 2 (polyptoton) cites Vǫlundarkviða 23.3 bróðir á bróður, Igor 77 rekosta bo bratŭ bratu 'brother spoke to brother', MBh. 6.44.2 bhrātā bhrātaram, Aesch. Sept. 674 κασιγνήτωι κάσις (not cognate) and Serbo-Croat brat brata. Parallels, checked locally: Old Russian, Slovo 77 (TOROT spi; NC corpus, so the parallel words only) рекоста ... братъ брату 'brother said to brother', followed by direct speech (nom. + dat.; the verb is the dual of the pair). Old Norse, Vǫlundarkviða 23 (FJ 1926) Snimma kallaði seggr á annan, bróðir á bróður: göngum baug séa 'early one man called to the other, brother to brother: let us go and see the ring' (nom. + á + acc.). Epic Sanskrit, MBh 3.158 (DCS sentence 9) bhrātā bhrātaram āsīnam abhyabhāṣata 'the brother addressed the seated brother' (nom. + acc. with abhi-bhāṣ). West's MBh 6.44.2 is 'brother did not recognize brother', not an address, so this DCS passage stands in for it. In all three the polyptoton of *bʰréh₂tēr frames a speech act. Secure: *bʰréh₂tēr, exact in all three (ORuss. bratъ, ON bróðir, Skt. bhrātṛ-). Interpolated: the verb. The three verbs are not cognate (ORuss. rešti, ON kalla, Skt. bhāṣ-), and the engine's reduplicated aorist wéwket 'said' (Ved. ávocat, Gk εἶπε) stands in none of the passages. Case: the dative of the addressee follows the Old Russian; ON and Sanskrit put the accusative after a preposition or preverb. Number: 3sg with ON and Sanskrit, against the Slovo's dual. Late witnesses: the Slovo is 12th-century at the earliest and its authenticity is debated; the Mahābhārata is post-Vedic. Limits: kin-term polyptoton is a widespread figure (West also lists 'friend to friend', 'man to man'), and the Old Russian may echo Church Slavonic biblical idiom. The core is one lexeme in a figure, with no shared verb.

plan.english: You are the son of Sky.

notes: 'Son of Sky': the genitive of the sky-god with *suHnús. West 2007 ch. 4 equates the Baltic Sons of God (Lith. Diẽvo sūnẽliai, Latv. Dieva dēli) with the Vedic Aśvins (Divó nápātā RV 1.182.1; Divó ... putráḥ 1.181.4) and the Dioskouroi; only Vedic and Lithuanian use *suHnús for 'son'. Parallels, checked locally: Vedic, RV 3.25.1 ágne diváḥ sūnúr asi 'Agni, you are the son of Sky' (vedaweb). Lithuanian, Rhesa (1843 ed.) no. 48 'Szaltinatis' O atėjo Diewo Sunelei / su szilkū tinkleleis 'And the Sons of God came with silken nets' (the Baltic divine twins; the Sun's daughters are in the same song; local OCR, old orthography). Greek, Il. 16.522 Σαρπηδὼν Διὸς υἱός (AGDT; Il. 1.9, of Apollo, as support). Late witness: the daina is a 19th-century record, valid for the wording only. Secure: the genitive *diwés, exact in Vedic diváḥ and Greek Διός. Lith. Dievo is the genitive of Dievas < *deywós, the same root but another lexeme: root level. Head *suHnús: exact only in Vedic sūnú-. Lith. sūnẽlis is a diminutive of sūnùs, and Greek υἱός is *suH-yú-, another formation of the same root: both root level. The builder's 'exact' for υἱός is a false positive (its reflex table equates υἱός with *suHnús). Referents differ: Agni (Vedic), Sarpedon (Greek), the divine twins (Lithuanian). The claim is for the title's wording, not for one figure. Frame: the predicate with the copula follows RV 3.25.1 (2sg h₁ési); Greek and Lithuanian have the noun phrase as subject or apposition. Interpolated: the copula. Overlaps divine-twins-001 and sky-father-010 in the genitive 'of Sky' only; this line's head is the shared 'son' word, which those lines lack.
